case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal courts may recognize (or should refuse to recognize) a private aiding-and-abetting cause of action under the Alien Tort Statute (and relatedly how, if at all, the TVPA informs that question), particularly when the alleged assistance involves U.S. corporations and misconduct occurring abroad.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 28 U.S.C. § 1350 (Alien Tort Statute); Torture Victim Protection Act of 1991 (TVPA), Pub. L. No. 102-256, 106 Stat. 73 (codified as a note to 28 U.S.C. § 1350).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Cisco (and supporting amici) argue that courts should not extend the judicially implied ATS cause of action to cover aiding-and-abetting liability, emphasizing separation-of-powers concerns and the Court’s recent skepticism about expanding ATS remedies. They contend that recognizing aiding-and-abetting claims would amount to creating new forms of civil liability not authorized by Congress, would intrude on the political branches’ control of foreign affairs, and would force U.S. courts to pass on the legality of foreign sovereign conduct. Petitioners also invoke the general presumption against implying civil aiding-and-abetting liability absent clear congressional direction (drawing on Central Bank), and argue that the TVPA’s carefully specified cause of action counsels against broader judge-made secondary liability under the ATS.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (the Doe plaintiffs, as reflected by the framing of the dispute in the government’s description and the Ninth Circuit posture referenced in the materials) maintain that aiding-and-abetting claims are available under the ATS’s limited, Sosa-recognized framework for certain well-defined international-law norms, and that secondary liability is a traditional and appropriate feature of tort-based accountability for grave human-rights abuses. They argue that allowing ATS aiding-and-abetting claims is consistent with historical understandings of international-law violations (and enforcement mechanisms), necessary to provide a remedy where direct perpetrators may be foreign officials or otherwise unreachable, and compatible with Sosa’s two-step approach (identify a sufficiently definite international-law norm and then consider prudential/foreign-policy limits). They also resist the view that the TVPA implicitly forecloses ATS secondary liability, instead treating the TVPA as complementary rather than restrictive.
key_precedents: Jesner v. Arab Bank, PLC, 584 U.S. 241 (2018)
Nestlé USA, Inc. v. Doe, 593 U.S. 628 (2021)
Central Bank of Denver, N.A. v. First Interstate Bank of Denver, N.A., 511 U.S. 164 (1994)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Jackson make the best case that, once Sosa permits a narrow set of judge-made ATS claims, aiding-and-abetting can be treated as an ordinary “remedial incident” necessary to make those claims workable when principals are unreachable. But Sosa’s instruction to proceed with “great caution,” coupled with Jesner and Nestlé’s separation-of-powers and foreign-relations warnings, cuts against taking the additional, policy-laden step of recognizing a freestanding secondary-liability regime absent a clear congressional signal. Justice Sotomayor is right that Central Bank arose in a different statutory posture, yet its default rule against inferring private civil aiding-and-abetting from silence has special force where the ATS is jurisdictional and the TVPA shows Congress legislates expressly when it wants secondary liability. A narrow holding that the ATS does not authorize civil aiding-and-abetting liability without congressional action preserves Sosa’s limited primary-violator claims while respecting institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that aiding-and-abetting can be treated as a mere “remedial incident” necessary to make Sosa’s narrow ATS claims workable. But under an originalist and textualist approach, the threshold problem remains: § 1350 supplies jurisdiction only, and neither its text nor its original public meaning authorizes federal courts to create new private causes of action, let alone a secondary-liability regime; calling it “remedial” does not supply the missing congressional authorization. Central Bank’s rule against inferring private civil aiding-and-abetting liability from silence reinforces that courts exceed their role when they invent such liability, and the TVPA’s express, calibrated cause of action (including defined contours) confirms that Congress “knows how” to create liability in this domain and did not do so in the ATS. As Justice Gorsuch emphasizes, Sosa’s admonition of “great caution,” coupled with Jesner and Nestlé’s separation-of-powers and foreign-affairs concerns, counsels against extending judge-made ATS litigation to aiding-and-abetting absent a clear statutory directive.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s best point is that aiding-and-abetting could be treated as a mere “remedial incident” needed to make Sosa’s narrow ATS causes of action workable when principal wrongdoers are unreachable. But under a textualist approach, that framing does not answer Central Bank’s baseline rule—emphasized by the Chief Justice—that civil aiding-and-abetting is not presumed from silence, and the ATS is not merely silent but jurisdictional, so recognizing secondary liability would be an additional, policy-laden layer of judge-made liability. Justice Barrett’s TVPA point reinforces the separation-of-powers problem: Congress expressly calibrated liability (including secondary liability) when it chose to legislate in this area, which counsels against our adding an ATS aiding-and-abetting regime with the foreign-relations consequences flagged in Jesner and Nestlé. The respondents’ case-by-case limiting principle (Sosa caution plus U.S. nexus) sounds administrable in theory, but it still leaves courts making the threshold legislative choice to expand liability—precisely what Sosa’s “great caution” and our recent ATS cases instruct us to avoid absent clear congressional authorization.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Central Bank is the strongest point for Petitioner, but I do not think its presumption against implied aiding-and-abetting carries over cleanly to the ATS after Sosa: we are not enlarging a congressionally created private right but operating in the narrow federal-common-law space Sosa already recognized, where courts must supply ordinary modes of responsibility to make the limited cause of action workable. Justice Barrett’s TVPA negative-implication argument likewise reads too much into Congress’s decision to provide an express remedy for torture/extrajudicial killing; that looks like ratification and calibration for those specific wrongs, not a clear instruction to strip secondary-liability principles from the separate ATS framework Sosa preserved. I share Justice Kavanaugh’s foreign-relations and institutional concerns, but those are better handled through Sosa’s “great caution,” rigorous mens rea/substantial-assistance requirements, and Nestlé’s domestic-conduct/nexus constraints than through a categorical bar that predictably leaves victims without any remedy when principal perpetrators are unreachable. On my pragmatic approach attentive to real-world consequences for vulnerable plaintiffs, Petitioner’s bright-line rule risks under-enforcing universally condemned norms without a clear congressional command to do so.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s Central Bank point is the most serious challenge, but I agree with Justice Sotomayor that it does not translate cleanly to the Sosa posture: Central Bank refused to infer a new, policy-laden liability term into a congressionally crafted implied right, whereas Sosa already recognizes a narrow federal-common-law cause of action and necessarily leaves courts to supply ordinary incidents of adjudication that make it workable. Justice Barrett’s TVPA negative-implication argument is a meaningful cautionary signal, but it reads too much into Congress’s choice to create an express torture remedy; it is not a clear instruction to strip the Sosa-preserved ATS space of familiar modes of responsibility for other definite norms. And while Justice Gorsuch is right to stress “great caution” and the foreign-relations concerns in Jesner and Nestlé, I see those cases as prescribing tightening principles (domestic nexus, sensitivity to diplomatic friction, rigorous mens rea/assistance requirements), not a categorical bar that would often nullify Sosa’s narrow set of claims in practice. On my pragmatic textualist approach, treating aiding-and-abetting as a mode of liability within the limited Sosa cause of action is the more coherent and administrable reading than declaring it an impermissible ‘expansion’ whenever the text is jurisdictional.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s best point is that, once Sosa permits a narrow class of federal-common-law ATS claims, courts must supply ordinary “remedial incidents” like aiding-and-abetting to make those claims workable. But that reframing still assumes Article III courts have affirmative authority to create a distinct civil secondary-liability regime when the ATS’s text is jurisdictional and supplies no cause of action; under my textualist/originalist approach, that is precisely the sort of lawmaking Sosa said must proceed with “great caution,” and Jesner/Nestlé underscore the foreign-affairs costs of further judge-made expansion. Chief Justice Roberts’s Central Bank analogy remains persuasive not because it mechanically controls, but because it reflects a broader separation-of-powers baseline: absent a clear congressional signal, we do not infer civil aiding-and-abetting, and the case for restraint is even stronger where Congress has shown (in the TVPA) it knows how to specify secondary liability expressly. Justice Sotomayor’s under-enforcement/workability concerns are serious, but they go to policy and cannot supply the missing statutory authorization.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s “remedial incident” framing is the strongest argument for Respondent, because it highlights that some secondary-liability principles can be necessary to make Sosa’s narrow causes of action workable when primary perpetrators are unreachable. But in my institutionalist reading of Sosa as narrowed by Jesner and Nestlé, recognizing aiding-and-abetting is not just filling in remedial details—it is a consequential, policy-laden extension of judge-made exposure in an area with acute foreign-relations sensitivity, and those cases repeatedly warn that further ATS expansions are for Congress. Chief Justice Roberts’s Central Bank point matters here even if the doctrinal posture differs: it supplies a baseline presumption against inferring a private civil aiding-and-abetting regime from silence, and that presumption has special force where the ATS is jurisdictional and Congress (as Justice Barrett notes via the TVPA) has shown it can expressly calibrate secondary liability when it chooses. Sosa-caution and nexus tests, as Justice Sotomayor proposes, are not a sufficient limiting principle because they still require courts to make the threshold legislative choice to create a new layer of liability with predictable diplomatic and separation-of-powers costs.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s best argument is that, once Sosa permits a narrow federal-common-law cause of action, aiding-and-abetting should be treated as an ordinary “remedial incident” rather than a separate norm. But even accepting Sosa’s limited carve-out, that move still requires an additional, lawmaking step—creating a secondary-liability regime—without textual footing in a statute that is jurisdictional, and Central Bank’s presumption against civil aiding-and-abetting from silence remains a powerful default in the absence of a clear congressional signal. Justice Sotomayor’s workability/under-enforcement concern is weighty, yet under an originalist/textualist methodology it cannot supply authority where the statute does not, and Jesner and Nestlé amplify why we should be especially reluctant to expand judge-made liability in a foreign-relations-sensitive area. The TVPA’s express calibration reinforces that Congress can and does speak to secondary liability when it chooses, which counsels against our supplying it here by implication.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s Central Bank point is the strongest push, but it is a default rule about not enlarging a congressionally created private right from statutory silence; here, under Sosa we are already in a narrowly cabined federal-common-law remedial space where courts must supply ordinary incidents of liability to make a recognized norm enforceable. Justice Barrett’s TVPA negative-implication argument is not a clear withdrawal of that limited authority: the TVPA can reasonably be read as a targeted, supplemental cause of action for torture/extrajudicial killing rather than a silent command to excise familiar secondary-liability principles for other Sosa-qualifying norms. I take Justice Kavanaugh’s Jesner/Nestlé foreign-relations concerns seriously, but in my view they counsel rigorous nexus/extraterritorial limits and a demanding mens rea/substantial-assistance standard, not a categorical bar that would often leave plaintiffs without any practical remedy when principal perpetrators are unreachable. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers framing does not persuade me to switch because refusing all aiding-and-abetting, absent clear congressional direction, risks making Sosa’s already narrow pathway functionally illusory in the very cases where enforcement is most needed and where careful judicial gatekeeping can do the work.

John Roberts.reasoning: The ATS is "a jurisdictional statute creating no new causes of action," and Sosa instructs that any judge-made ATS remedy must be limited to a modest set of claims grounded in a "specific, universal, and obligatory" international-law norm and recognized only with "great caution" as a matter of judicial discretion. Recognizing a freestanding private aiding-and-abetting cause of action would extend ATS liability beyond the narrow historical paradigms and risk the kind of foreign-relations and separation-of-powers concerns emphasized in Jesner and Nestlé, particularly where the alleged assistance involves U.S. corporate conduct connected to harms occurring abroad. Central Bank further counsels against implying civil aiding-and-abetting liability absent clear congressional direction, and the TVPA’s carefully specified cause of action suggests Congress knows how to authorize secondary liability when it chooses, reinforcing the case for judicial restraint here. A narrow disposition declining to extend ATS remedies to aiding-and-abetting best preserves institutional legitimacy and respects Congress’s role in defining new civil liability touching foreign affairs.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Alien Tort Statute, 28 U.S.C. § 1350, is purely jurisdictional and contains no text creating any cause of action—much less a secondary-liability regime for aiding and abetting—so federal courts exceed their Article III role when they recognize such claims without congressional authorization. Under Central Bank of Denver, statutory silence does not permit courts to infer private civil aiding-and-abetting liability; Congress “knows how” to provide it when it wishes, and it did not do so in the ATS. Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain confirms that any ATS-based cause of action is at most a narrow, cautious judicial undertaking, and Jesner v. Arab Bank and Nestlé USA, Inc. v. Doe underscore that expanding ATS liability—especially in ways that implicate foreign affairs and extraterritorial conduct—should be left to Congress. The TVPA’s express, carefully delimited cause of action further indicates Congress legislates expressly in this area, counseling against courts creating broader judge-made secondary liability under the ATS.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The ATS, 28 U.S.C. § 1350, is jurisdictional and does not textually supply a private cause of action—Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain permits only a narrow, cautious set of judge-made claims and counsels strong hesitation before expanding remedies with foreign-affairs implications. Recognizing a freestanding civil aiding-and-abetting theory would be an additional step beyond Sosa’s limited framework and would conflict with the presumption that civil aiding-and-abetting liability is unavailable absent clear congressional authorization, as emphasized in Central Bank of Denver v. First Interstate Bank. The TVPA’s express, carefully delineated cause of action underscores that when Congress wants to create liability for international-law violations, it knows how to do so, and it did not authorize ATS secondary liability—especially where the alleged misconduct and primary actors are abroad, raising the separation-of-powers and international-friction concerns highlighted in Jesner and Nestlé. Prudentially and as a matter of practical consequences, allowing such claims would invite broad litigation against U.S. companies for overseas conduct and entangle federal courts in sensitive foreign-policy disputes better left to Congress and the Executive.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain recognizes that, although the ATS is jurisdictional, federal courts may supply a limited common-law cause of action for a “modest number” of well-defined international-law violations, exercised with “great caution.” Within that narrow Sosa framework, aiding-and-abetting liability can be understood as part of the remedial apparatus for enforcing established norms (e.g., torture, extrajudicial killing), especially where primary perpetrators abroad are effectively unreachable and victims would otherwise be left without any meaningful civil remedy. The TVPA’s express cause of action for torture and extrajudicial killing (codified as a note to 28 U.S.C. § 1350) is best read as complementary—not silently preclusive of ATS secondary liability—because it reflects Congress’s acceptance of civil accountability for grave abuses rather than a command to strip courts of traditional tort principles where Sosa already permits a claim. While Jesner and Nestlé caution against expansive ATS innovation and emphasize foreign-relations limits, those concerns are addressed by demanding a sufficiently specific international-law norm and a strong U.S. nexus, not by categorically foreclosing aiding-and-abetting liability in all ATS cases involving U.S. corporate assistance to atrocities abroad.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain recognizes a narrow, cautious federal-common-law cause of action under the ATS, limited to well-defined and universally accepted international-law norms, and it contemplates that courts must also apply traditional restraint and workability limits in fashioning the remedial framework. Within that limited Sosa framework, allowing aiding-and-abetting liability is best understood as a remedial incident of enforcing a qualifying norm, not the recognition of a new substantive international-law norm, and it is consistent with tort principles needed to make the remedy workable where direct perpetrators are often beyond reach. Central Bank’s presumption against implied aiding-and-abetting liability is context-specific and does not control the ATS’s unique common-law setting recognized in Sosa, especially where the claim remains tightly cabined by Sosa’s “great caution” requirement and the extraterritorial limits emphasized in Nestlé. The TVPA’s express cause of action (codified as a note to 28 U.S.C. § 1350) does not clearly foreclose ATS secondary liability for other Sosa-qualifying norms; absent such a clear directive, and given the ATS’s limited role, I would not read the TVPA to impliedly narrow the remedial tools available under § 1350.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Alien Tort Statute, 28 U.S.C. § 1350, is a jurisdictional provision and does not by its text create causes of action, much less a distinct secondary-liability regime for aiding and abetting. Under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain, any judge-made ATS remedy must be approached with “great caution,” and our more recent decisions underscore that courts should not expand ATS liability in ways that risk foreign-affairs consequences and legislative displacement (Jesner; Nestlé). Separately, Central Bank teaches a strong default rule: federal courts should not infer private civil aiding-and-abetting liability from statutory silence, and nothing in the ATS supplies the clear congressional authorization that rule demands. The TVPA’s express, carefully delimited cause of action further confirms that when Congress wishes to create human-rights civil liability (and define its contours), it knows how to do so, making it inappropriate for courts to invent broader secondary liability under the ATS.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Alien Tort Statute, 28 U.S.C. § 1350, is jurisdictional, and under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain federal courts may recognize only a narrow set of historically grounded claims with great caution given foreign-affairs and separation-of-powers concerns. Extending the ATS to a judge-made aiding-and-abetting cause of action—especially for overseas misconduct—would be a significant expansion of implied liability that Congress has not authorized, and it risks the very practical and diplomatic problems highlighted in Jesner and Nestlé. Central Bank counsels against presuming civil aiding-and-abetting liability absent clear congressional direction, and the TVPA’s specific, congressionally crafted cause of action further suggests courts should not create broader secondary-liability regimes under the ATS. Given this Court’s recent ATS decisions and the need for institutional restraint, I would refuse to recognize an ATS aiding-and-abetting cause of action here.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The ATS, 28 U.S.C. § 1350, is jurisdictional and does not by its text create a cause of action, and under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain federal courts may recognize only a narrow set of claims with great caution and deference to Congress, especially where foreign-relations consequences are foreseeable. Recognizing a private aiding-and-abetting theory would extend the judicially implied ATS remedy beyond what the statute authorizes, and Central Bank of Denver holds that courts should not infer private civil aiding-and-abetting liability from statutory silence when Congress knows how to provide it expressly. The TVPA’s express cause of action and its calibrated scope (including explicit secondary-liability language) reinforces that Congress legislates expressly in this area, counseling against a broader judge-made secondary-liability regime under the ATS. Jesner and Nestlé further underscore separation-of-powers and extraterritoriality concerns that weigh against expanding ATS remedies, particularly for corporate assistance tied to misconduct abroad.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain, 28 U.S.C. § 1350 is jurisdictional but permits a narrow set of federal common-law causes of action for well-defined and universally accepted international-law norms, and the remedial question (including secondary liability) should be assessed pragmatically within that limited framework rather than categorically foreclosed. Aiding-and-abetting liability can function as a traditional incident of tort-based accountability where direct perpetrators are unreachable, so long as the underlying norm is sufficiently definite and the claim satisfies the ATS’s extraterritorial limits emphasized in Nestlé USA, Inc. v. Doe. The TVPA’s express cause of action for torture and extrajudicial killing does not, by negative implication, bar ATS aiding-and-abetting for other Sosa-qualifying norms; it is more naturally read as complementary, and refusing any secondary liability would risk denying effective remedies for grave abuses without a clear congressional command. Prudential and foreign-relations concerns highlighted in Jesner v. Arab Bank can be addressed through Sosa’s “great caution” and case-specific limits, rather than an across-the-board rule that federal courts may never recognize aiding-and-abetting under the ATS.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal courts may recognize aiding-and-abetting liability under a judicially implied cause of action in the Alien Tort Statute (and how, if at all, the TVPA informs that analysis), particularly when the alleged assistance involves U.S. companies’ conduct connected to human-rights abuses abroad.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Alien Tort Statute (ATS), 28 U.S.C. § 1350; Torture Victim Protection Act of 1991 (TVPA), 28 U.S.C. § 1350 note.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Cisco and related defendants) argue that courts should not create or extend ATS causes of action to include aiding-and-abetting claims because doing so is judicial lawmaking with serious foreign-relations consequences; they emphasize the Court’s recent ATS decisions narrowing implied liability, contend that there is at least a strong presumption against civil aiding-and-abetting liability absent clear authorization (invoking Central Bank), and maintain that any further expansion should be left to Congress (with the TVPA’s limited, express cause of action suggesting restraint).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Doe plaintiffs) contend that aiding-and-abetting liability is a recognized, settled feature of modern ATS litigation consistent with Sosa’s framework for limited recognition of international-law norm violations; they argue that international law norms against complicity in grave human-rights abuses support secondary liability, that recognizing such claims is necessary to provide a remedy where defendants knowingly provide substantial assistance to overseas abuses, and that neither the ATS nor the TVPA forecloses aiding-and-abetting theories where the pleaded norms and factual allegations satisfy Sosa and subsequent limitations.
key_precedents: Jesner v. Arab Bank, PLC, 584 U.S. 241 (2018)
Nestlé USA, Inc. v. Doe, 593 U.S. 628 (2021)
Central Bank of Denver, N.A. v. First Interstate Bank of Denver, N.A., 511 U.S. 164 (1994)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that aiding-and-abetting is a traditional “mode of liability” rather than a new international-law norm—still does not answer the threshold institutional question whether federal courts may supply a domestic civil secondary-liability regime on top of Sosa’s already tightly constrained, judge-made ATS cause of action. As Justice Thomas emphasizes with Central Bank, we generally do not presume civil aiding-and-abetting liability from silence, and that separation-of-powers caution applies with even greater force where the underlying remedy is itself implied and where, under Jesner and Nestlé, foreign-relations consequences are substantial. Justice Jackson’s effort to cabin Central Bank as merely “statutory” does not persuade me because the core concern is judicial lawmaking absent congressional authorization, not the label on the source of law. The TVPA’s express, carefully delimited framework reinforces that Congress knows how to create and define human-rights civil liability, so a narrow holding declining to recognize ATS aiding-and-abetting absent congressional direction best preserves institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that aiding-and-abetting is merely a “mode of liability” and not a “new norm”—does not cure the threshold defect that § 1350’s text is jurisdictional and contains no authorization for courts to supply remedial and secondary-liability rules; under an original public meaning approach, that is legislative work. Even if international law recognizes some concept of complicity, translating it into domestic civil aiding-and-abetting requires us to choose elements (mens rea, causation, substantial assistance) and scope, which is exactly the additional lawmaking Sosa cautioned against and that Jesner and Nestlé warn has serious foreign-relations consequences. Justice Jackson’s attempt to cabin Central Bank to statutory remedial schemes is unpersuasive because the separation-of-powers principle against implying civil aiding-and-abetting from silence applies with greater force where the underlying cause of action is itself judge-made. As the Chief Justice notes, the TVPA’s express, calibrated cause of action confirms Congress knows how to create and delimit human-rights civil liability when it intends to, and we should not expand the ATS by implication.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s core point—that aiding-and-abetting is simply part of the international-law “enforcement architecture” for Sosa-qualifying norms—does not resolve the separation-of-powers problem because § 1350 is jurisdictional and contains no textual authorization for a private damages remedy, much less secondary liability; international law can inform conduct and responsibility, but it cannot supply Congress’s decision to create a cause of action in U.S. courts. Even accepting Justice Sotomayor’s framing of aiding-and-abetting as a “mode” rather than a “new norm,” recognizing it would still require federal courts to choose mens rea, substantial-assistance, and causation standards, compounding the judicial lawmaking Sosa warned against and amplifying the foreign-relations concerns emphasized in Jesner and Nestlé. Central Bank’s presumption against implying civil aiding-and-abetting from statutory silence applies a fortiori here, where the primary ATS cause of action is itself implied; layering implied secondary liability atop an implied remedy is exactly the institutional escalation we should avoid. As Chief Justice Roberts notes, the TVPA’s express, calibrated scheme confirms Congress knows how to authorize and delimit human-rights liability, which counsels restraint rather than further judicial invention under the ATS.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan make the strongest institutional point that, under Sosa, courts must be cautious about adding doctrinal “layers” with foreign-relations consequences, and I accept that any ATS extension demands restraint. But I do not think recognizing aiding-and-abetting is an “additional norm” in the Sosa sense; it is a familiar mode of liability that enforces an already Sosa-qualifying, specific and universal prohibition, and the hard lines can be policed by Sosa’s vigilant doorkeeping plus Nestlé’s domestic-conduct limits and comity considerations. Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Central Bank does not move me because it addressed implying secondary liability within a congressionally designed statutory remedial scheme, whereas ATS claims (if any) operate as narrowly constrained federal common law tied to international-law-defined wrongs—so the separation-of-powers concern is addressed by refusing to expand actionable norms, not by categorically disabling ordinary responsibility principles. The TVPA’s express cause of action, as Roberts argues, underscores Congress’s capacity to legislate precisely, but it does not clearly foreclose courts from applying traditional secondary-liability principles when doing so does not broaden the set of actionable norms and remains subject to our recent limits in Jesner and Nestlé.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point—that aiding-and-abetting is a familiar mode of liability rather than a “new norm”—does not, for me, solve the antecedent problem Sosa identifies: § 1350 is jurisdictional, and any ATS cause of action is already a cautiously implied remedy, so layering a secondary-liability regime still requires judicial choices about mens rea, substantial assistance, and scope that are not anchored in the statute’s text. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito are right that Central Bank’s presumption against implying civil aiding-and-abetting from silence is not just a technical rule of one statutory scheme but reflects a broader institutional reluctance to create expansive remedial doctrines without congressional authorization—especially where the primary cause of action is itself judge-made. Justice Jackson’s attempt to cabin Central Bank as “statutory” is thoughtful, but it underestimates how much remedial design here (and the foreign-relations friction flagged in Jesner and Nestlé) turns precisely on domestic judicial lawmaking rather than on international-law specificity. The TVPA’s express, calibrated cause of action reinforces that Congress knows how to authorize and delimit human-rights civil liability when it chooses, which counsels restraint rather than judicial supplementation under the ATS.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “mode of liability” framing is the strongest pushback, but even if complicity is recognized in some form in international law, importing it here still requires us to craft a domestic civil secondary-liability rule (mens rea, substantial assistance, causation) without textual footing in § 1350—precisely the incremental lawmaking Sosa says to approach with great caution and that Jesner and Nestlé warn against in this foreign-relations-laden context. I am not persuaded by Justice Jackson’s effort to cabin Central Bank to statutory schemes, because the separation-of-powers concern is, if anything, sharper when we would be layering an implied aiding-and-abetting doctrine atop an already-implied ATS cause of action. Chief Justice Roberts’s point about the ATS’s jurisdictional character and the need for restraint reinforces that we should not take this additional step absent clear congressional authorization. The TVPA’s express, calibrated remedial design remains a strong signal that Congress knows how to specify the scope of liability for human-rights abuses and that courts should not expand ATS remedies by implication.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s strongest point—that aiding-and-abetting is a traditional “mode of liability” that can ride along with a Sosa-qualifying norm—still does not answer the institutional question of who gets to choose the elements of that secondary-liability regime in ATS cases. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, importing civil aiding-and-abetting would require us to make consequential, policy-laden choices about mens rea, substantial assistance, and causation on top of an already judge-made cause of action, in a domain (foreign relations) where Jesner and Nestlé tell us to be especially cautious. Central Bank’s presumption against implied civil aiding-and-abetting liability, relied on by Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch, applies with even greater force here because the ATS remedy itself is implied—layering implied doctrines compounds the separation-of-powers problem. The TVPA’s tailored scheme, as multiple colleagues note, is better read as Congress’s decision to specify when and how secondary liability should exist, not as an invitation for us to extend ATS liability by judicial innovation.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the strongest point that aiding-and-abetting is a “mode of liability” embedded in enforcement of established norms rather than a freestanding new norm. But even accepting that framing, it does not answer the antecedent domestic question: § 1350’s text supplies jurisdiction only, and recognizing a civil aiding-and-abetting theory still requires federal courts to select elements (substantial assistance, causation) and mens rea—an additional, consequential layer of judge-made remedial law that Sosa, and especially Jesner and Nestlé, tell us to approach with extreme caution in foreign-relations-sensitive litigation. Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s emphasis on remedial authority is decisive for me, and Central Bank’s presumption against implying civil aiding-and-abetting from silence applies with special force where the primary cause of action is already implied rather than congressionally specified. The TVPA’s express, cabined cause of action reinforces that Congress knows how to authorize and delimit liability rules in this area, so I do not read its silence as delegating to courts the further step of creating secondary liability under the ATS.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s institutional caution—especially the worry that recognizing aiding-and-abetting would force courts to craft mens rea, substantial-assistance, and causation standards in a foreign-relations-sensitive area—squarely presents the hardest point for my position. But that concern is overstated if we treat secondary liability not as an invitation to broaden the set of actionable norms, but as an ordinary incident of enforcing a Sosa-qualifying, universally obligatory norm, with additional constraints supplied by Jesner and Nestlé (domestic conduct/comity) and by Sosa’s own “vigilant doorkeeping.” Justice Thomas’s and Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Central Bank does not genuinely undermine my analysis because that presumption operated within a congressionally designed statutory remedial scheme, whereas ATS claims (to the limited extent Sosa allows them) are federal common-law implementations of international-law norms where complicity can be part of the accepted liability architecture. The TVPA’s express remedy, emphasized by Justice Alito and Justice Barrett, is a reason to police the boundaries carefully, not to adopt an across-the-board bar that would pretermit norm-by-norm inquiry and potentially immunize knowing facilitators of universally condemned offenses where the claim otherwise satisfies Sosa.

John Roberts.reasoning: The ATS, 28 U.S.C. § 1350, is “jurisdictional” and does not itself create causes of action; under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain, any judicial recognition of new ATS claims must be tightly constrained and exercised with “great caution,” especially where foreign-relations consequences are substantial. Extending an implied ATS cause of action to encompass aiding-and-abetting liability would be a further step in judicial lawmaking that this Court has repeatedly resisted in the ATS context, see Jesner v. Arab Bank and Nestlé USA, Inc. v. Doe, both emphasizing separation-of-powers and the need for restraint when suits touch conduct abroad. The TVPA’s express, limited cause of action (with Congress specifying who may be sued and for what) reinforces that any expansion of civil liability for human-rights abuses—including secondary liability—should come from Congress, not from courts implying additional doctrines into the ATS.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Alien Tort Statute, 28 U.S.C. § 1350, is a jurisdictional grant and contains no textual authorization for a private cause of action, much less for secondary aiding-and-abetting liability; recognizing such liability would require judicial lawmaking inconsistent with the Constitution’s allocation of lawmaking power to Congress. Under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain, any judicial recognition of ATS causes of action must be tightly constrained, and this Court’s subsequent decisions (Jesner v. Arab Bank and Nestlé USA, Inc. v. Doe) underscore that courts must not extend implied ATS liability in ways that intrude on foreign affairs and exceed the statute’s original public meaning. Central Bank of Denver rejects inferring civil aiding-and-abetting liability from statutory silence, and nothing in the ATS’s text overcomes that presumption here. The TVPA’s express, carefully delimited cause of action confirms that when Congress intends to create liability for human-rights abuses it does so expressly, counseling against expanding the ATS by implication to reach aiding-and-abetting theories against U.S. companies for conduct connected to abuses abroad.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The ATS is a jurisdictional statute, and under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain federal courts may recognize only a narrow set of implied causes of action, exercising “vigilant doorkeeping” and special caution where foreign-relations consequences are substantial. Extending that judge-made framework to include civil aiding-and-abetting liability goes further still, and Central Bank of Denver v. First Interstate Bank establishes the default rule that civil aiding-and-abetting liability is not available absent clear congressional authorization—authorization the ATS does not provide. The TVPA underscores that point: when Congress wanted to create an express federal cause of action for torture and extrajudicial killing, it did so explicitly and in a limited way, counseling restraint in expanding ATS implied liability. Given this Court’s recent narrowing approach in Jesner and Nestlé, the safer, more textually grounded course is to leave any new secondary-liability regime to Congress.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain, the ATS is jurisdictional but permits a narrow class of federal common-law claims for violations of specific, universal, and obligatory norms, subject to "vigilant doorkeeping" and prudential caution about foreign-relations concerns. Aiding-and-abetting liability is best treated not as an adventurous "new norm," but as an accepted mode of enforcing well-defined prohibitions (e.g., torture, extrajudicial killing) where a defendant knowingly provides substantial assistance, and the TVPA’s express cause of action for torture and killing supports—rather than undermines—the availability of traditional secondary-liability principles when those same grave norms are at issue. Central Bank’s presumption against implied aiding-and-abetting in a statutory scheme is not controlling here because ATS causes of action, if any, arise from federal common law implementing international-law norms, not from judicial augmentation of a comprehensive statutory remedial scheme. Consistent with Nestlé USA, Inc. v. Doe, the suit still must satisfy limits on extraterritoriality and domestic conduct, but categorical rejection of aiding-and-abetting would unnecessarily foreclose remedies for vulnerable victims where U.S.-connected actors allegedly facilitate egregious abuses.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The ATS is “jurisdictional” and does not itself create causes of action, so under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain courts may recognize only a narrow set of claims with great caution and with close attention to separation-of-powers and foreign-relations concerns. Extending that already-implied ATS cause of action to encompass aiding-and-abetting liability is a further judicial step not clearly grounded in the statute’s text, and this Court’s more recent ATS cases (Jesner and Nestlé) underscore reluctance to expand implied ATS liability in ways that risk diplomatic friction. The TVPA’s express, carefully delimited cause of action suggests that when Congress intends to authorize civil liability for human-rights abuses (and specify its contours), it does so directly—counseling judicial restraint rather than enlargement of implied remedies under § 1350. Given those constraints, the better course is to leave any new secondary-liability regime under the ATS to Congress.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Alien Tort Statute, 28 U.S.C. § 1350, is a jurisdictional grant and does not by its plain text create a cause of action, so any judicially implied liability—especially a secondary aiding-and-abetting theory—raises acute separation-of-powers and foreign-relations concerns under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain and Jesner v. Arab Bank. Central Bank of Denver instructs that civil aiding-and-abetting liability is not presumed from statutory silence and requires clear congressional authorization, a rule that applies with even greater force where the underlying cause of action is itself judicially implied. The TVPA’s express, carefully cabined cause of action for torture and extrajudicial killing confirms Congress knows how to create liability (and to define its scope) and counsels against expanding ATS remedies by judicial invention. Consistent with Nestlé USA, Inc. v. Doe, further extension of ATS liability—particularly to encompass aiding-and-abetting claims tied to overseas abuses—should be left to Congress, not federal courts.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain, the ATS is a jurisdictional statute and any judicially implied cause of action must be narrowly cabined, with courts exercising restraint especially where foreign-relations consequences are substantial. Recognizing civil aiding-and-abetting liability would be a significant expansion of implied ATS liability, and Central Bank of Denver v. First Interstate Bank counsels that civil aiding-and-abetting is not presumed absent clear congressional authorization—an institutional concern that applies with even greater force in the ATS context. Jesner v. Arab Bank and Nestlé USA, Inc. v. Doe further emphasize separation-of-powers limits and the need for caution given diplomatic friction when U.S. courts adjudicate overseas human-rights disputes; if secondary liability is to be authorized, Congress is better positioned to do so. The TVPA’s express, carefully limited cause of action underscores that Congress knows how to create human-rights remedies and suggests courts should not broaden ATS implied remedies beyond what Congress has specified.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The ATS is “strictly jurisdictional” and does not itself create causes of action; under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain courts may recognize only a “very limited” set of claims with great caution, mindful of separation-of-powers and foreign-relations consequences. Extending a judicially implied ATS remedy to include aiding-and-abetting liability would require additional lawmaking—defining secondary liability standards and mental-state requirements—precisely the sort of step Sosa, Jesner, and Nestlé warn courts not to take absent clear congressional authorization. Central Bank reinforces the presumption against inferring civil aiding-and-abetting liability without express statutory text, and the TVPA’s express, limited cause of action (and Congress’s choice of express terms there) counsels restraint rather than further implied expansion under § 1350.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Sosa v. Alvarez-Machain, 542 U.S. 692 (2004), federal courts may recognize a narrow class of ATS claims tied to specific, universal, and obligatory international-law norms, and that inquiry can encompass well-established secondary-liability principles where the pleaded norm includes complicity in grave abuses. Central Bank of Denver, 511 U.S. 164 (1994), addressed implied aiding-and-abetting liability under a particular statutory scheme and does not categorically bar courts from recognizing aiding-and-abetting theories when the ATS cause of action is itself defined by international-law norms rather than by Congress’s enumerated elements. The TVPA’s express cause of action (28 U.S.C. § 1350 note) confirms Congress’s acceptance that U.S. courts may provide civil redress for certain human-rights violations and does not clearly foreclose ATS aiding-and-abetting liability for other Sosa-qualifying norms; any remaining separation-of-powers and foreign-relations concerns are better handled through Sosa’s “practical consequences” and limiting-principles analysis rather than an across-the-board prohibition. Consistent with Jesner v. Arab Bank and Nestlé USA, Inc. v. Doe, the claim must still satisfy the Court’s constraints (including careful attention to domestic conduct and comity), but I would not categorically reject aiding-and-abetting liability as a matter of law.
